https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8r6.text: Figure caption, Rescuers race to free people trapped after building collapse in Delhi By Geeta Pandey and Arunoday Mukharji Reporting from BBC News, Delhi Published 6 September 2026 Updated 6 hours ago Rescuers are digging through the rubble a day after a residential building collapsed in the Indian capital, Delhi, killing at least seven people. It's not clear how many people were inside the five-storey building in south-west Delhi - or if there are still people under the debris. Eyewitnesses told local media on Sunday that two-to-four dozen people were inside, but no official numbers have been shared. Authorities have confirmed 12 people were taken to hospital and that seven died while others are receiving treatment. Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said "accumulation of water, combined with ongoing repair work in the basement" of the building, Hostel Daze, caused the collapse. The building owner has been arrested and five senior civic officials of Delhi Municipal Corporation (MCD) have been suspended following the tragedy, Gupta added. The building in the Satya Niketan neighbourhood of south-west Delhi, which sits a short distance from Delhi University's south campus which has five colleges, came down around 13:30 local time (08:00 GMT) on Sunday. A majority of the residents were students and many were thought to be in their rooms at the time of the collapse as there were no lessons on Sunday. On Monday morning, Gupta said "approximately 80% of the debris had been cleared" from the building, and "only the rubble from the basement remains". The BBC found the area around the site of the collapse cordoned off and teeming with rescue workers in bright orange uniforms. An excavator dug through the rubble in the hope of finding survivors amidst a pile of bricks. In another corner, a few mattresses half covered in debris were lying in a pile. The smell of burning metal was overpowering as teams of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) could be seen using electric saws to cut through iron grills, penetrating layers and layers of steel and concrete. There is no confirmation if there are still people under the debris or if there are more survivors. Hospital officials are not saying whether the casualties include students, local residents or labourers who were working in the basement. Image source, Charlotte Scarr/ BBC Image caption, The area around the site of the collapse has been cordoned off and police and rescue workers have been deployed On Sunday, a local legislative assembly member at the scene said that some of the trapped students had been making calls from under the rubble. An eyewitness who was at his shop nearby when the tragedy struck told news agency ANI that the building collapse sounded "like the rumble of an earthquake". "We rushed out immediately; there was a lot of smoke and dust here. The entire building had collapsed. Some bodies were recovered, and they also rescued four students who were still breathing." He said he could hear students crying out from under the rubble saying "save us, save us!" Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure" - and local media reports say it would be demolished on Monday. "Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added. Delhi Police said the building had only been 40 or 50 years old. The owner of a nearby shop told ANI that it had been under a 100-year lease and that the leaseholder had undertaken excavation work in the basement to expand the hostel and increase their income. A civic official said they were trying to ascertain whether any digging or structural work was carried out in the building recently, Times of India reported. , external "Given the incessant rain, we are examining the possibility of seepage weakening the structure. Repair or other work could also have contributed to the collapse. At this stage, however, it is difficult to establish the exact cause," he said. Police have registered a case against the owner of the building and are searching for him. Image source, Reuters Image caption, With hostel spaces in short supply, many students who move to Delhi to attend South Campus colleges live in private hostels and paying-guest accommodation The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate the cause of the collapse and hold anyone found responsible to account. "Negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated at any cost," it said. Satya Niketan is a densely populated area which houses a large student population, with a number of hostels in the neighbourhood. Many students who come from outside Delhi to attend South Campus colleges are forced to live in cheap private hostels and paying-guest (PG) accommodations due to a lack of hostel facilities on campus. "There are 75 students in Sociology Honours class, but only two get a seat in the college hostel. All other students have to live here," Sawai Sharma, a student of Venkateswara College, told BBC News Hindi. Sharma, who often visited a friend who lived in the building and narrowly escaped the accident, said a bed in the building cost 18,000 rupees ($190; Â£140) a month, making it affordable for students. Another student, Shivam Yadav, said a friend of his lived in the building and was in his room at the time of the accident. "He was on the third floor at the time of the accident. He has been rescued and sent to hospital." Yadav said that most of the buildings in Satya Niketan are "overloaded". "The buildings are in a dilapidated condition. No inspections are conducted. There are no rules or guidelines here." College student Ankit Tiwari said conditions at these hostels and PGs "are appalling". "Students are paying a lot for a very small space which they share with others. There is no proper water or sewage facility here." Tiwari, who lives nearby, reached the site about half an hour after the collapse. "Students were helping each other as we came first, before the rescue teams arrived. What we saw was tragic. We have been finding books, mangled desks and study notes," he said. Building collapses are relatively common in Delhi, with more than a thousand recorded in the past three years causing dozens of deaths, according to fire department figures. Poor foundations, inadequate materials and unqualified construction workers were among the common reasons for collapses. Eleven people, including three children, were reportedly killed last April when a residential building collapsed in north-eastern Delhi. In 2024, three students drowned after getting trapped in the flooded basement of an exam coaching centre in capital Delhi, sparking anger and protests. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Thirty-four people have been killed by alligators in Florida since 1948. Photograph: Bruce Bennett/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Thirty-four people have been killed by alligators in Florida since 1948. Photograph: Bruce Bennett/Getty Images Florida Florida fisher dragged into water and killed by 12ft alligator Steve Hamilton was fishing in Winter Garden when he was attacked by gator, which was later killed Eric Berger Sat 17 Oct 2026 11.23 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 13.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man fishing at a pond in Florida was killed on Friday by an alligator that was almost 12ft long in a rare kind of animal attack, according to authorities and media reports. Steve Hamilton, 71, was on the shoreline in the community of Winter Garden when the animal dragged him into the water, the Florida news outlet WOFL reported , citing local police and the state’s fish and wildlife conservation commission. Emergency crews responded to the park where Hamilton was fishing at about 5.20pm on Friday after receiving a 911 call and attempted to rescue him – but they had difficulty doing so because of nearby alligators, the outlet reported. Hamilton’s body was recovered from the water a couple of hours later. Capt Michael Mason of the Winter Garden police department told news media that the alligator had been killed after the fatal attack on Hamilton. Authorities were not alerted of a gator sighting on Friday at the pond, which is connected to Lake Apopka, Mason said. The body of water has “tons of alligators in it. That is not uncommon to see alligators in this part of town,” Mason said. The chief encouraged people to “be aware of your surroundings”. The gator “looks like it’s docile. It looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous,” Mason said. Alligator attacks are statistically rare. Nonetheless, at least 34 people have been killed by them in Florida since 1948, according to the Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission , which compiles reports of encounters with the state’s estimated 1.3 million gators. Hamilton’s death came less than four months after a woman named Brittany Clark was attacked and killed by a 13ft alligator while swimming with her boyfriend in the Econlockhatchee River in Florida’s Seminole county. Autopsy results released in July showed Clark, 31, struggled for her life before dying from the wounds inflicted on her by the alligator, which was removed from the river and euthanized. After Clark’s death, the Republican US House member Greg Steube of Florida introduced a resolution calling for the federal comptroller general and the US Department of the Interior to study how American alligators’ being listed as “threatened due to similarity of appearance” to crocodiles affects his state’s ability to remove nuisance gators from residential and commercial waterways. Steube said the species has been fully recovered since 1987, but it remains protected to prevent the trafficking and hunting of the similar-looking American crocodile. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: View image in fullscreen ‘If you don’t shower, so what?’ The western diplomats staying put in under-attack Kyiv Thomas Lund-Sørensen: ‘It’s cognitive warfare … They are trying to influence public opinion in my country.’ Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Ambassadors say presence sends powerful signal of solidarity and support amid escalation in Russian strikes and warnings Luke Harding in Kyiv; photographs by Julia Kochetova Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Last modified on Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.35 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he warning from Moscow was blunt. Western diplomats should immediately leave the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv . If they failed to do so they would be “in mortal danger”. The statement added that Russia would not responsible for any “potential negative consequences” if its advice was ignored. European envoys in Kyiv responded to the Kremlin’s threat last month with a loud raspberry. Denmark’s ambassador to Ukraine, Thomas Lund-Sørensen, took to social media to say that he was staying . So did the ambassadors from Germany, Italy, Spain, Sweden, France, Poland and Estonia . Even the Americans indicated they would not be budging. View image in fullscreen Denmark’s ambassador, Thomas Lund-Sørensen, said the Russians were trying to spook Europeans to undermine support for Ukraine. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Speaking at his embassy office, decorated with a Lego Cossack warrior, Lund-Sørensen said the Russians were trying to spook Europeans in order to undermine support for Ukraine . “It’s cognitive warfare. These attacks have been going on for a long time. They are trying to influence public opinion in my country. Of course we will continue here,” he said. The ambassador admitted that his job had scary moments, shared by all in Kyiv . “If you don’t find it frightening when 10 ballistic missiles hit within a couple of minutes you should probably go and see someone,” he said, but added: “There is a difference between being in uncomfortable and life-threatening situations. If you don’t shower, so what?” View image in fullscreen Borded up windows, signs of Russian attacks near the EU delegation office. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian View image in fullscreen On Friday, a Russian drone crashed into a hospital in central Kyiv, a few hundred metres from the Danish embassy. Photograph: Alessio Mamo/The Guardian The decision to remain in a city under fire is not without risk. On Friday, a drone crashed into a hospital in central Kyiv , the institute for orthopaedics and traumatology, a few hundred metres from Lund-Sørensen’s workplace. The bang could be heard for miles around. Russia has dramatically stepped up its attacks since August, hurling missiles and hundreds of jet-powered drones . Major urban centres such as Kharkiv and Odesa have suffered, too. Seemingly frustrated by failure to progress on the battlefield, the Kremlin has intensified its all-out campaign against civilians. It has targeted bridges across the Dnipro river , thermal heating plants and substations, as well as trains and railway stations . Power cuts last most of the day. In the past week, there was no water for 24 hours. The bombing has reached the historic centre of Kyiv, where many embassies are located. In October the German consulate was damaged in an attack that killed eight people. View image in fullscreen Power cuts last most of the day in Ukrainian cities such as Kyiv. Photograph: Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto/Shutterstock In 2025, two missiles landed in the car park next to the EU delegation building. Deadly metal cubes perforated its ground floor, shattering armoured windows. The strike was at dawn, before staff arrived. Nobody was hurt. This September, a drone exploded 500 metres away. Debris ravaged the ninth-floor, bringing down glass, ceiling panels and the ventilation system. “I was in a meeting with seven colleagues. We ran to the corridor,” said Katarína Mathernová, the EU’s ambassador in Kyiv. “I’ve never heard anything that loud in my life. There were plumes of smoke. It was shocking.” The delegation is now reinforcing its outer walls with sandbags. It has put beanbags in corridors, for staff to use during air raids. There are foldable beds and extra showers. Asked whether the Kremlin wanted to murder diplomats, as opposed to merely scaring them a little, Mathernová replied with a quote from Catch 22, Joseph Heller’s famous satirical novel. “As Yossarian says: ‘They are trying to kill me! They are lobbying bombs at us!’ I think they are warning shots. They [the Russians] are more and more brazen and callous.” View image in fullscreen ‘The level of attacks are much higher than last year, and the power cuts earlier,’ Katarína Mathernová said. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Vladimir Putin’s strategic goal, she added, was to destroy the EU. She described Russia’s latest threat as “intimidation”, made in the hope that some diplomats from the global south might abandon Kyiv. Meanwhile, the city was creaking. “The level of attacks are much higher than last year, and the power cuts earlier. We’ve had no water in our building. The soft underbelly of a modern city is its sewage system,” she said. As the capital braces for winter, ambassadors say their continued presence sends a powerful signal of solidarity to Ukraine’s embattled leadership. “They tell us thank you for being here,” Lund-Sørensen said. A fellow ambassador added: “We would all like to stay. We feel conscious that our presence is politically and psychologically important for Ukraine and its resilience.” The envoy said that in his view the Russians were not hitting foreign missions “by design”. He thought, however, that “sooner or later” a diplomat would be killed by a drone “falling in the wrong place” – an act that would plunge that country’s government into crisis, as it mulled how to respond to Putin’s violence and disregard for international law. For visiting prime ministers and presidents, getting to and from Kyiv has become more dangerous . The capital’s airport has been shut since the 2022 invasion. Train or car are the only options. On a recent journey from Poland, the envoy said he had to leave his rail compartment twice because of marauding drones. “I sat in the woods for one and a half hours. The train staff gave me a biscuit,” he said. Frequent air alerts and attacks on bridges have disrupted embassy business and made it difficult for local Ukrainian staff to get to work, he added. The envoy acknowledged: “I have a privileged existence. An alarm goes off and I go and sleep in the basement. Ukrainians have adapted their security protocols. But it’s more inconvenient. There’s a degree of nervousness.” View image in fullscreen Millions of Ukrainians are forced to sleep in bomb shelters, corridors and on the cold floors of metro stations. Photograph: Alina Smutko/Reuters Mathernová said she sleeps on a mattress in the bathroom of her hotel suite during Russian strikes. She pointed out that millions of Ukrainians are forced to do the same thing – kipping down in bomb shelters, corridors and on the cold floors of metro stations. “There is nothing funny about using winter as a weapon of mass destruction,” she posted earlier this year, after a Kremlin official mocked a photo of her in pyjamas . Kyiv is classified as a hardship role. Western ambassadors typically stay for two years, separated from families. Lund-Sørensen said there was not exactly “a queue” of colleagues wanting to work in Ukraine but enough “right people” volunteered. “It’s really hard to imagine as a diplomat a more meaningful posting than Ukraine. Its struggle against Russia is personal to me and my country,” he said. At weekends the envoy relaxes by going on long cycle rides. Mathernová said she enjoyed Nordic walking in the botanical gardens , as well as saunas and dinners with friends. “Kyiv has an unbelievable array of amazing restaurants. One of the things I will miss most is its culinary scene. And it’s can-do attitude. Everything is possible. It’s a big contrast with Brussels,” she said. Luke Harding’s Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest is published by Guardian Faber.
